title: BUG: Fix segfault in MT19937 by preventing recursive seed lists
body:
PR summary
This PR fixes a Segmentation Fault (stack overflow) that occurs when initialising MT19937 with a recursive or self-referencing list.
Previously, passing a cyclic list (e.g., x = []; x.append(x)) into the generator caused an infinite loop in the Cython unpacking logic, leading to a hard crash.
I added a _has_cycle helper function in bit_generator.pyx to detect self-referencing sequences early. If a cycle is detected, the SeedSequence initialisation now safely raises a ValueError instead of segfaulting.

Closes #28822 
First-time committer introduction
Hi everyone! I am a newer contributor looking to dive deep into the Python data science stack. I wanted my first major contribution to be on the systems level rather than just documentation, so hunting down a C/Cython memory bug seemed like a great challenge. I'm excited to learn more from the maintainers here!

AI Disclosure
I used an AI assistant (Google Gemini) strictly as a pair-programming tool to help navigate the Meson/Spin build system and to draft the initial logic for the _has_cycle helper function. I manually compiled the environment, reproduced the bug, and verified the fix locally.

### Verification
Here is the local terminal output proving the fix. Instead of a Segmentation Fault, it now safely catches the cycle and throws the expected exception:

```bash
Testing MT19937...
Traceback (most recent call last):

Sourced from hypothesis's releases.

Hypothesis for Python - version 6.152.9

This release substantially improves our internal distribution for generating integers. This release has the most visible effect on "integers()", but may incidentally improve other strategies which draw integers internally.

Our integers distribution had two problems. First, it had jagged discontinuities at certain values where we switched sampling approaches. Second, it used a different distribution for bounded and unbounded ranges, which resulted in "st.integers()" and "st.integers(-264, 264)" producing very different distributions despite being semantically similar.

We now use a smooth distribution for both "st.integers()" and "st.integers(a, b)", which fixes both of these issues. This should substantially improve our testing power in certain cases.

The only way this release should be user-visible is that it finds more bugs! If this release is user-visible in other ways - for example, because it is slower, or produces a worse distribution in some cases - please open an issue.

Fixes https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/31762

This PR fixes the crash on 32 bit systems when using abi3t ABI. In this PR, the first member of the `PyArrayDescr` is now aligned to 8 bytes so that regardless of the size of the actual `PyObject`, the field accesses remain correct. 8 bytes is used instead of `alignof(max_align_t)` to preserve backwards compatibility with exisiting abi3 extensions where `sizeof(PyObject)` is a multiple of 8 thereby the added alignment is no-op and does not changes the offset for such extensions.

title: Dealing with opaque API, 32bit builds and Fields Getting
body:
Let's maybe move the discussion here @da-woods, @kumaraditya303, and @ngoldbaum.

Right now to allow opaque API use, we have a family of:
* `(PyArray|*)_GET_ITEM_DATA` static inline function which use,
* A family of `_*` functions that all do the same thing (remove `PyObject *` offset for the build).
* A family of `_fields` structs that omit `PyObject *`.

As noticed by Nathan in gh-31759 this doesn't work for 32bit free-threaded builds, the reason is that `sizeof(PyObject) < sizeof(max_align_t)` meaning that the `_fields` struct may have a different layout.

There are two approaches plausible:
1. Forgo `_GET_ITEM_DATA` completely...  *everything* would have to go through actual API functions.
2. Rather adding `PyObject` to our types, we add `PyObject_made_multiple_of_max_align_t`.

My gut feeling is:  Doing 1 would basically reduce the whole current approach to rubbles and make NumPy less convenient than a full opaque API using module (where *Python* would add that same padding as @da-woods pointed out).

My current take is that we should go with 2 and pad on Python 3.15+, this breaks ABI for free-threaded 32bit builds, but that release doesn't exist yet.
(After thinking, I suspect Cython is actually OK, since it just uses the `sizeof()` from the header and doesn't care if there is an additional field conditional to the Python version.)


I'll be annoying and actually ask @da-woods once if you think the family of functions is worth it.
Sorry, it still feels a bit unnecessary to me. Yes, it allows inserting private fields at the start which is cute, but only if we ever break the non opaque ABI fully for that same object.  (But yeah, I guess I am the only one who feels this way so whatever...)

title: BUG: descriptor accessors should account for struct padding on 32bit abi3t builds

labels.name: 39 - free-threading
labels.description: PRs and issues related to support for free-threading CPython (a.k.a. no-GIL, PEP 703)

body:
This was first seen in https://github.com/PyO3/rust-numpy/pull/556

The `flags` field of the `PyArray_Descr_fields` struct is explicitly 64 bits:

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/6d68c69402a0eb5bd03e82485e86b92a917c08b6/numpy/_core/include/numpy/ndarraytypes.h#L649-L650

On the 32-bit free-threaded build, `sizeof(PyObject)` is 20 bytes. On the 32 GIL-enabled build it's 8 bytes.

The combination of these facts have annoying implications for 32-bit Python abi3t builds, given our current field access implementation.

On the free-threaded build, `type_num` is at 28 bytes, so `flags` is at 32 bytes and no padding is necessary. On the 32 bit GIL-enabled build, the `type_num` starts at offset 16, so `flags` must be padded from 20 to 24 bytes to stay 8-byte aligned.

This throws off the way we implemented access for `flags` and all fields after `flags` on abi3t, since all accesses go through the `_PyDataType_GET_ITEM_DATA` function and there are now two different offsets we need to deal with for `flags` and every field after.

I think at a minimum we need to add at least one new API function to account for whether or not the padding bytes exist for accesses on `flags` and all fields after `flags`. On abi3t, the offset calculation needs to happen in NumPy internals, and it's the only place that can know at runtime if the interpreter is free-threaded or not.

On 64 bit, the PyObject sizes on free-threaded and GIL-enabled builds are 32 bytes and 16 bytes, respectively. These are both 8-byte aligned and we don't notice this issue.

I had an attempt at a fix for this in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/31759. The fix is wrong (it breaks the GIL-enabled 32 bit build) but the test I added might be helpful.

title: BUG: aligned access for the descriptor fields struct on 32bit abi3t

labels.name: 39 - free-threading
labels.description: PRs and issues related to support for free-threading CPython (a.k.a. no-GIL, PEP 703)

body:
Over in https://github.com/PyO3/rust-numpy/pull/556 work is ongoing to add abi3t support for crates that depend on PyO3 and rust-numpy.

There is [a failing test run](https://github.com/PyO3/rust-numpy/actions/runs/27867012031/job/82473307007?pr=556) for win32 3.15t, in a test that accesses the `metadata` field for a datetime dtype instance.

I was able to track this down to the uint64 `flags` field on the `PyArray_Descr_fields` and `_PyArray_LegacyDescr_fields` structs.

On a 32 bit free-threaded build, `sizeof(PyObject)` is 20 bytes. That places the `flags` field at a 4-byte aligned address instead of an 8-byte aligned address, the compiler inserts some padding bytes, and suddenly the fields access function is returning addresses at the wrong offset for all fields *after* the `flags` entry.

The fix I landed on was to define the `flags` as two 32 bit integers. Each gets read individually, and the compiler inserts no more packing bytes into the struct. Inside the `flags` access macro, we re-assemble the lo and hi parts of the 64 bit int.

Also adds a static assert in case a future change to `sizeof(PyObject)` breaks our assumptions here. Also adds a regression test to access the datetime metadata field, like the rust-numpy test did.

I used Claude to help identify and fix this bug.

Release notes

Sourced from hypothesis's releases.

Hypothesis for Python - version 6.152.9

This release substantially improves our internal distribution for generating integers. This release has the most visible effect on "integers()", but may incidentally improve other strategies which draw integers internally.

Our integers distribution had two problems. First, it had jagged discontinuities at certain values where we switched sampling approaches. Second, it used a different distribution for bounded and unbounded ranges, which resulted in "st.integers()" and "st.integers(-264, 264)" producing very different distributions despite being semantically similar.

We now use a smooth distribution for both "st.integers()" and "st.integers(a, b)", which fixes both of these issues. This should substantially improve our testing power in certain cases.

The only way this release should be user-visible is that it finds more bugs! If this release is user-visible in other ways - for example, because it is slower, or produces a worse distribution in some cases - please open an issue.

title: BUG: restore ndarray.conjugate() for legacy user-defined dtypes
body:
### PR summary

#31264 rewrote PyArray_Conjugate to dispatch to the conjugate ufunc only when the DType defines an `imag_meth` slot, dropping the explicit `PyArray_ISUSERDEF` route. Legacy user dtypes have no `imag_meth` and are not flagged numeric, so `arr.conjugate()` began raising "cannot conjugate non-numeric dtype" in 2.5.0, even when a conjugate ufunc loop is registered (e.g. numpy-quaternion).

Restore the legacy user-dtype route so these dtypes dispatch to the ufunc as before, while leaving the new-style view/numeric behavior intact.

Closes #31754


#### AI Disclosure
I used Claude to find where the original bug came from, and to check through the docs and commit history to convince myself that this was the right approach.

title: ENH: Expand abstract DType hierarchy
body:
Introduces ``NumericAbstractDType`` and a fuller numeric "kind" tree mirroring the array-API hierarchy:

    NumericAbstractDType
        IntegerAbstractDType
            SignedIntegerAbstractDType
            UnsignedIntegerAbstractDType
        InexactAbstractDType
            FloatAbstractDType
            ComplexAbstractDType

The new abstract DTypes are exposed on ``numpy.dtypes`` and the legacy concrete DTypes inherit from them so ``isinstance``/``issubclass`` reflect the kind hierarchy.

Adds ``register()`` on abstract DTypes for legacy/user-defined DTypes to opt into a kind, with custom ``__subclasscheck__`` / ``__instancecheck__`` on the metaclass consulting the registered cache and the ``NPY_DT_NUMERIC`` flag.

``np.isdtype`` now uses and accepts DType classes (including these abstracts), although passing a non-instance as first argument is deprecated as I think it is a bit wonky.
(Do allow the scalar types as they map OK, but... really that shouldn't be the normal use-case, I think.)

(I used a bit of AI to implement some larger patterns, and some of the tests are; I'll go through once more myself as well.)

title: BUG: ndarray.conjugate() regression for legacy user-defined dtypes in 2.5.0
body:
### Describe the issue:

`ndarray.conjugate()` (and `.conj()`) raises `TypeError: cannot conjugate non-numeric dtype` for legacy (pre-NEP-42) user-defined dtypes in NumPy 2.5.0. It worked in 2.4.x and earlier. This affects any dtype registered via `PyArray_RegisterDataType`, including ones that register their own `conjugate` ufunc loop. The `np.conjugate(arr)` *ufunc* is unaffected — only the `ndarray.conjugate()`/`.conj()` *method* regressed.

The example below uses NumPy's own in-tree `rational` test dtype, so it needs no third-party packages:

- **2.4.6:** `a.conjugate()` → `[1 2 3]` (no-op, correct for this real-valued dtype)
- **2.5.0:** `a.conjugate()` → `TypeError: cannot conjugate non-numeric dtype`

A real-world case is [numpy-quaternion](https://github.com/moble/quaternion), whose dtype registers a genuine `conjugate` ufunc loop; `arr.conjugate()` used to compute the quaternion conjugate via that loop and now errors (moble/quaternion#270).

**Root cause:** #31264 / commit b6bc683 ("ENH: Allow user-dtypes return views on `.conjugate()`") rewrote the dispatch in
`PyArray_Conjugate` (`numpy/_core/src/multiarray/calculation.c`):

```diff
-    if (PyArray_ISCOMPLEX(self) || PyArray_ISOBJECT(self) ||
-            PyArray_ISUSERDEF(self) || !NPY_DT_is_legacy(PyArray_DESCR(self))) {
+    if (NPY_DT_SLOTS(NPY_DTYPE(PyArray_DTYPE(self)))->imag_meth != NULL) {
```

The old condition routed user-defined dtypes (`PyArray_ISUSERDEF`) to the `conjugate` ufunc. The new one routes only dtypes whose DType defines an `imag_meth` slot. Legacy user dtypes have no `imag_meth` (a NEP-42/43 slot) and are never flagged `NPY_DT_NUMERIC` (for legacy descriptors that flag is set only when `PyTypeNum_ISNUMBER(descr->type_num)`, always false for `type_num >= NPY_USERDEF`), so they fall through to the new `!NPY_DT_is_numeric(...)` branch and error — even when a `conjugate` loop is registered.

(For clarity: the `"cannot conjugate non-numeric dtype"` *message* predates this and came from the expired no-op-fallthrough deprecation; that expiry was fine, since in 2.4.x the `PyArray_ISUSERDEF` carve-out kept user dtypes off that path. The regression is specifically the removal of that carve-out in #31264, which doesn't appear to have been intended to change legacy-dtype behavior.)

**Expected behavior:** as in 2.4.x — dispatch to the registered `conjugate` ufunc loop if one exists, otherwise return a view (real-valued no-op). Legacy user dtypes should not unconditionally error.


### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import numpy as np
from numpy._core._rational_tests import rational

a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=rational)
print("dtype:", a.dtype, "type_num:", a.dtype.num)  # rational 256
print("np.conjugate (ufunc) works:", np.conjugate(a))  # [1 2 3]
print(a.conjugate())  # TypeError on 2.5.0, was [1 2 3] on 2.4.6
```

### Error message:

```shell
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-0>", line 7, in <module>
    print(a.conjugate())  # TypeError on 2.5.0, was [1 2 3] on 2.4.6
          ~~~~~~~~~~~^^
TypeError: cannot conjugate non-numeric dtype
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

2.5.0
3.14.6 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Jun 12 2026, 08:47:56) [Clang 20.1.8 ]


### Runtime Environment:

  'python': '3.14.6 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Jun 12 2026, 08:47:56) '
            '[Clang 20.1.8 ]',

                      'found': ['ASIMDHP', 'ASIMDDP'],

Found via a downstream bug report against the quaternion package (moble/quaternion#270): a user's array-conjugation code that worked on numpy <= 2.4.6 began raising TypeError on 2.5.0. The same regression reproduces on NumPy's own in-tree `rational` dtype, so it affects any legacy user-defined dtype, not just quaternion.

title: ENH: Implement MaskedArray.tofile()
body:
`MaskedArray.tofile()` was not implemented and always raised `NotImplementedError`. That also meant `np.save()` failed on masked arrays, since it ends up calling `tofile()`.

This delegates to `filled(fill_value).tofile()`, same as `tobytes()`. Masked entries are written using the fill value; the mask itself is not stored in the file.

Updated the stub in `core.pyi` and replaced the old test that only checked for `NotImplementedError`.

title: BUG: restrict weak scalar handling in resolve_dtypes to input operands
body:
### PR summary
This PR fixes a SegFault in `ufunc.resolve_dtypes` for calls like: `np.sin.resolve_dtypes((int, int))`

The bug:
- `int`/`float`/`complex` were treated as weak scalar markers in all operand positions.
- This means for output operands as well. This is invalid for those. And, it results in a segfault.

Fix:
- Restrict weak-scalar handling to input operands only.
- For output operands, builtin int/float/complex are interpreted as concrete NumPy dtypes.

Result:
- `np.sin.resolve_dtypes((int, int))` now raises a normal casting error (`UFuncOutputCastingError`) instead of crashing.
- Valid weak input behavior remains unchanged (e.g. `np.sin.resolve_dtypes((int, None))`).

Tests:
- Updated unary weak-scalar resolve_dtypes test coverage.

### First time committer introduction
Hi all, I am new to the NumPy community. I use NumPy mainly in my data science, and graph theory projects. I wanted to make contributions to open source, and my procrastination finally ended recently. I was thinking of contributing to something I use regularly, and that's how I chose NumPy (I use it regularly). 

### AI Disclosure
- I used ChatGPT Go and OpenAI Codex (gpt-5.3-codex medium effort) to help with debugging and fixing the issue.
- I manually created the development environment, built numpy from source, reviewed, edited, and validated all code and tests.

Closes #31734

Release notes

Sourced from hypothesis's releases.

Hypothesis for Python - version 6.152.9

This release substantially improves our internal distribution for generating integers. This release has the most visible effect on "integers()", but may incidentally improve other strategies which draw integers internally.

Our integers distribution had two problems. First, it had jagged discontinuities at certain values where we switched sampling approaches. Second, it used a different distribution for bounded and unbounded ranges, which resulted in "st.integers()" and "st.integers(-264, 264)" producing very different distributions despite being semantically similar.

We now use a smooth distribution for both "st.integers()" and "st.integers(a, b)", which fixes both of these issues. This should substantially improve our testing power in certain cases.

The only way this release should be user-visible is that it finds more bugs! If this release is user-visible in other ways - for example, because it is slower, or produces a worse distribution in some cases - please open an issue.

title: TYP: specialized ``conj[ugate]``, ``reciprocal``, and ``square`` ufuncs
body:
Following #31741, here's another batch of ufunc specializations, targeting the unary endo-ufuncs on `number | object_`; `conj[ugate]`, `reciprocal`, and `square`. 

Boolean input, although not in the type signature, required additional overloads, since boolean input results in `int8` output, so it couldn't be "absorbed" in the `int_` overloads like with the other specialized ufuncs (`sin` for example).

I also snuck in a tiny fix, so that obscure array-likes that aren't captured by any of the other overloads, will also be accepted if no `dtype` or `out` param is required. This is probably pretty rare in the wild (e.g. no related mymy primer errors), but it's an easy fix, so we might as well.

---

No AI.

title: TYP:  mypy reports `error: "TypeAliasType" not callable` when creating arrays with `numpy.ma.masked_array` since numpy v2.5
body:
### Describe the issue:

Running the code example below through mypy with the command `pixi x --with numpy=2.5 mypy --verbose myproblem.py` gives the following error:
```
LOG:  Mypy Version:           2.1.0
...
myproblem.py:3: error: "TypeAliasType" not callable  [operator]
```

It looks like this happens because `masked_array` is defined as a type alias in this file:
https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.5.0/numpy/ma/core.pyi#L2851
while the code works fine because it is also defined as an alias in
https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/v2.5.0/numpy/ma/core.py#L6856
but `mypy` doesn't seem to understand that.

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import numpy as np

a = np.ma.masked_array([1])
```

### Error message:

```shell
myproblem.py:3: error: "TypeAliasType" not callable  [operator]
```

Python 3.14
Numpy 2.5

title: BUG: `ufunc.resolve_dtypes` segfaults
body:
I was trying to figure out how to use `ufunc.resolve_dtypes`. So as per usual, I threw away the manual and instead just tried a couple of guesses.

First I tried passing `1` to `np.sin.resolve_dtypes`, that didn't work:

```
In [1]: np.sin.resolve_dtypes(1)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[1], line 1
----> 1 np.sin.resolve_dtypes(1)

TypeError: resolve_dtypes: The dtypes must be a tuple of `ufunc.nargs` length.
```

The error message seems helpful though; it must be a tuple (of size 2 in this case), so I tried with `(1, 1)` next:

```
In [2]: np.sin.resolve_dtypes((1, 1))
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[2], line 1
----> 1 np.sin.resolve_dtypes((1, 1))

TypeError: Provided dtype must be a valid NumPy dtype, int, float, complex, or None.
```

Hmm, that didn't work either...
It mentions it accepts "dtype", I thought I'd try it with int *types*, i.e. `(int, int)`:

```
In [3]: np.sin.resolve_dtypes((int, int))
[1]    1121063 segmentation fault (core dumped)  ipython
```

😶 

---

I now realize that this works as intended with e.g. `resolve_dtypes((float, float))`.

This segfault clearly shouldn't have happened though; it should've raised a `TypeError` with a another helpful error message, like it did when I passed `(1, 1)` and `1`.

title: TYP: Fix incorrect dtype inference of ``asarray([])``
body:
There's a regression in 2.5.0 that caused `np.asarray([])`  to be inferred as a `bool` dtype, rather than `float64`. The fix is to move the relevant `float64` overloads before the `bool` ones (1d and 2d cases).

`np.array` and the other array constructors don't seem to have this issue; only `np.asarray`.

title: BUG: fix leak in reductions when a ufunc override errors or is not found
body:
### PR summary
Closes https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/31677

Just another thing I noticed while reading reduction code and realised there's an open issue for it already. 
One can see this memory leak by doing something like the following and memory profiling that (with memray for example) and will notice the memory is just growing.
```py
import numpy as np

class Array:
    data = np.array([1,2,3])
    def __array_ufunc__(ufunc, method, *inputs, **kwargs):
        return NotImplemented

arr = Array()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        try:
            np.add.reduce(arr)
        except Exception as e:
            pass
```
I think `goto fail` is probably nicer than
```c
Py_XDECREF(full_args.in);
Py_XDECREF(full_args.out);
```
and I believe it's safe. Only the `else if (override)` branch right bellow cannot use `goto fail` as it needs to return the override and not NULL.

I don't think there is a way to have a test regarding the ref count in the python side because `full_args` is created internally in the function in C. But we could have a test that is just the above without the loop and a sanitizer would probably capture the leak. Let me know if you want that. cc @seberg because you wanted a similar test in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/31699.

title: DEP: Deprecate `dot` for with more than 2 dimensions
body:
`np.dot()` and `arr.dot()` have a fun "dimension-interleaving" behavior for more than two dimensions.
In practice, this actually only matters when the second array has more than 2 dimensions (and the first more than one).

In that case, `dot` behaves like `tensordot(..., axes=[-1, -2])` and the result shape is something like `a.shape + b.shape "- axes"`.

This seems confusing and for most cases `tensordot` should be faster anyway because it lowers to BLAS (but may copy for reshaping) or `@/matmul` would be clearer (because it does outer broadcasting).

We should slowly deprecate the confusing paths or all >2D inputs. Probably deprecting all `>2D` because otherwise we need to add reshape or "use matmul" logic to get BLAS acceleration.

(This is related to/a follow up from gh-31575)

title: CI/TYP: Use Pyrefly to enforce 100% type coverage
body:
From https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/31710:

> Another cool thing is that pyrefly 1.1 comes with a new `pyrefly coverage check` feature. I wrote this as a better and more flexible alternative to `pyright --verifytypes`, which we're currently using in CI to prevent type-coverage backslides. So my plan is to follow this up with a PR that replaces `pyright --verifytypes`  with `pyrefly coverage check`, which will also allow us to get rid of the required pyright wrapper script to run it. I also expect that it will be a lot faster.

So this replaces the (based)pyright type completeness check with `pyrefly coverage check`, because it simply does a better job at measuring type coverage.

The default coverage threshold of `pyrefly coverage check` is set to 100%, which NumPy has, so there's no need to manually specify a `--fail-under=100` or something.

Relevant Pyrefly docs: https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/report/

The function signature defaults to `k=0`, and the description text explicitly calls `k` "an optional argument." However, the parameter type header was missing the standard NumPy `, optional` tag. 

This PR just updates `k : scalar` to `k : scalar, optional` to properly align the docstring with the actual function signature and NumPy's standard conventions.

title: TYP: specialized unary ``inexact | object_`` endo-ufuncs
body:
This is the first in a series of PRs where I'll be specializing individual (groups of) ufuncs so that they have proper typing support. Because currently, all ufuncs are (roughly speaking) annotated in the same "one size first all" way, causing all shape-typing and dtype information to be lost when they're used. 

I think this is the biggest typing-hole in numpy at the moment, but unfortunately it's going to be a lot of work to specialize each of the ufuncs. 

After experimenting (a lot) with this, I found that this "type-check-only subtyping" approach is the way to go (most robust, maintainable, and minimal differences between type-checkers). I've successfully been using this approach in scipy-stubs to specialize the `scipy.special` ufuncs, and so far I've had no issues with it, so it's a battle tested approach in that sense.

This is the first batch of ufuncs that tackles the 21 (excluding aliases) unary ufuncs with floating/complex/object input- and output-types (which is what I meant with "endo-ufuncs" in the title). As can be seen in https://gist.github.com/jorenham/d977c63cc53ad4f00878d37ee42ab0e8, it's the largest group of ufuncs sharing the same signature, so that's why I started with these ones. 

---

**TLDR**-ish;

For those that prefer code over my ramblings (so probabably everyone here), here's a quick little demonstration (using `pyrefly check`):

<details>
<summary>code for repro</summary>

```py
from typing import reveal_type

import numpy as np

reveal_type(np.sin(3.14))
reveal_type(np.sin([1, 2, 3]))
reveal_type(np.sin(np.eye(3, dtype=np.float64)))
```

</details>

*Before:*

(shape-type and dtype don't propagate)

```
 INFO revealed type: Any [reveal-type]

title: DOC: clarify the copy parameter of nan_to_num
body:
This updates the documentation of the `copy` parameter of `nan_to_num`, which still described the NumPy 1.x semantics.

Since `copy` is forwarded directly to `np.array`, its meaning is the same as everywhere else in NumPy: `True` always copies, `None` copies only when needed (replacing values in-place otherwise), and `False` raises a `ValueError` when a copy cannot be avoided. The previous wording suggested that `copy=False` would silently fall back to copying, which is no longer the case.

Closes #29045

title: TST: xfail multithreaded BLAS test more generously
body:
Fixes #31708.

xfail the test rather than noisily failing when we can't determine the BLAS library, either because we detect the netlib fallback version due to lack of threadpoolctl or because of a wrapper library like flexiblas.

This probably makes the test less useful for detecting buggy BLAS implementations but OpenBLAS is so ubiquitous it's going to be very noisy to make this test fail as often as I had written it originally.

title: BUG: fix StringDType distinct-allocator bugs and add tests (#31609)
body:
Backport of #31609.

Fixes bugs when multiple distinct stringdtype arrays are passed to `np.choose`, `np.put`, `np.putmask`, `np.place`, flatiter reads, and a bug that could lead to unsafe views being created for StringDType and object arrays.

Also exposes a new C helper function `_is_safe_view_cast` which takes `view_offset` into account and uses it in the Python helper functions for view safety. It only uses this function for StringDType. We could use it more generally but that might lead to breakage, so just fixing StringDType seemed like a practical first pass.

The C changes all work out to fixing the same couple patterns: legacy paths that used copyswap (e.g. #24859, which this might obviate the need for?) or code paths that assumed all input arrays have the same descriptor instance.

Also adds tests for functionality that is fixed here or is poorly tested currently. It makes use of a new helper function that allocates two distinct arrays of strings with allocations that live in the arena buffer to trigger these bugs.

I milestoned this for 2.5.0 and marked it for backport because these are all bugs that can cause segfaults.

I used Claude Fable 5 to work on this, including for the implementation and new tests.

title: ENH: Add np.EinsumExpression
body:
### PR summary

Closes #28394

Added `np.EinsumExpression` which is a callable class that pre-compiles einsum contraction paths. On repeated calls with the same shapes it skips subscript parsing and path optimization entirely

```python
expr = np.EinsumExpression('ij,jk,kl->il', (10, 20), (20, 5), (5, 10))
for _ in range(1000):
    result = expr(a, b, c)  # reuses pre-computed path
```

This uses `as_strided` with zero strides for path computation to avoid large allocations. Supports `out`, `dtype`, `order`, `casting` kwargs. Includes single-step optimization that uses `c_einsum` directly when the contraction has only one step.

### Benchmark 

| Benchmark | `einsum(optimize='greedy')` | `EinsumExpression` | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| matmul 4x4 | 26.3 us | 6.1 us | 4.33x |
| trace 4x4 | 27.3 us | 8.2 us | 3.32x |
| chain 20x30x40x20 | 151.5 us | 71.5 us | 2.12x |
| 5-operand chain | 190.5 us | 42.1 us | 4.52x |

Speedup mainly from eliminating repeated `einsum_path` computation and subscript parsing. Largest gains on small arrays and many-operand contractions where Python overhead matters the most

I can add release notes after this moves forward

body:
Closes https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/31691

... for _ in range(10000):
...     try:
...         np.add.accumulate(arr, out=out)
...     except Exception:
...         pass
... print(sys.getrefcount(out) - before)
...
10000 # with the fix, we get 0 here
```

title: BUG: out reference leak in PyUFunc_Accumulate and PyUFunc_Reduceat on type resolution failure
body:
## Bug Description

In both `PyUFunc_Accumulate` and `PyUFunc_Reduceat`, the `out` argument is INCREF'd early in the function, but when `reducelike_promote_and_resolve` fails immediately after, the code does `return NULL` directly — bypassing the `fail` label where `Py_XDECREF(out)` is located. This leaks the reference to `out`.

## Location

1. `numpy/_core/src/umath/ufunc_object.c`, `PyUFunc_Accumulate`, lines ~2745-2753
2. `numpy/_core/src/umath/ufunc_object.c`, `PyUFunc_Reduceat`, lines ~3168-3176

## Code

Both functions follow the same pattern:

```c
/* Take a reference to out for later returning */
Py_XINCREF(out);                          // line ~2745 / ~3168

PyArray_Descr *descrs[3];
PyArrayMethodObject *ufuncimpl = reducelike_promote_and_resolve(ufunc,
        arr, out, signature, NPY_TRUE, descrs, NPY_UNSAFE_CASTING,
        "accumulate");                     // or "reduceat"
if (ufuncimpl == NULL) {
    return NULL;                           // BUG: out's INCREF never balanced
}
```

Further down the function, the `fail:` label correctly does `Py_XDECREF(out)`, but the early `return NULL` bypasses it.

## Impact

Every time `accumulate()` or `reduceat()` is called with an `out` argument and type resolution fails (e.g., incompatible dtypes), the `out` array leaks a reference. Over repeated calls, this prevents the array from being garbage collected.

## Suggested Fix

Change `return NULL` to `goto fail` in both locations:

```c
if (ufuncimpl == NULL) {
    goto fail;
}
```

This ensures the `fail` label's cleanup runs, which includes `Py_XDECREF(out)`.

## Environment

- NumPy: current main branch
- Affected: `numpy.ufunc.accumulate()` and `numpy.ufunc.reduceat()` with `out` argument on type resolution failure

title: [BUG] out reference leak in PyUFunc_Accumulate on type resolution failure
body:
In `numpy/_core/src/umath/ufunc_object.c`, `PyUFunc_Accumulate` does `Py_XINCREF(out)` at line 2745. If `reducelike_promote_and_resolve` returns NULL right after (line 2751-2752), the code does `return NULL` directly instead of going through the `fail` label where `Py_XDECREF(out)` lives. So the INCREF is never balanced.

Same pattern exists in `PyUFunc_Reduceat` (lines 3168, 3174-3175).

Fix for both: change `return NULL` to `goto fail` so the cleanup path runs.

Checked on main branch as of 2026-06-17.

title: DOC: Update comment to advise keeping ``__dlpack__()`` v0
body:
### PR summary

This PR updates a comment in `dlpack.c` to advise against removing support for `__dlpack__()` version 0.

For the recently released nanobind v2.13.0, @wjakob observed that importing a NumPy array into a C++ Python module is 9% faster if `array.__dlpack__()` is called without specifying `max_version=(1, 0)`.  Furthermore, it is safe to do so when the module will only be reading from the array (i.e., on the C++ side the data is `const`).  Consequently, this is now done.  See: https://github.com/wjakob/nanobind/pull/1375/changes/439a0eb5db52009046ec767f8c75db3ac12ea854

Note that some (most?) frameworks (including older versions of NumPy) may return a `dltensor` regardless of whether the array is read-only or writable.  That's fine, again, since nanobind defaults to omitting `max_version` only when the C++ module wants only read access.

Currently, NumPy raises a BufferError if `array.__dlpack__()` is called on a read-only NumPy array.  In practice, it is believed that users typically do not `a.setflags(write=False)`.  If they do, nanobind will see the BufferError and try `array.__dlpack__(max_version=(1, 0))`, which will succeed.  [Sadly, the C++ module is slower when it wants read-only access to a read-only NumPy array than when it wants read-only access to a writable NumPy array.  When DLPack was first designed [PEP-3118](https://peps.python.org/pep-3118/)'s access flag `PyBUF_WRITABLE` was not yet well known.  DLPack version 1 added `DLPACK_FLAG_BITMASK_READ_ONLY`.]

Note that the performance results can be confirmed with Python 3.15.0b2 and NumPy 2.4.4.
First, version 0:
```
python -m timeit -n 10000000 -r 10 -s "import numpy as np; a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])" "a.__dlpack__()"
10000000 loops, best of 10: 51.3 nsec per loop
```
Then creating the tuple `(1,0)` once in the setup and timing with the keyword argument:
```
python -m timeit -n 10000000 -r 10 -s "import numpy as np; a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]); tpl=(1,0)" "a.__dlpack__(max_version=tpl)"
10000000 loops, best of 10: 68.9 nsec per loop
```

There may be better ideas and solutions moving forward, and I'd be happy if this PR is closed in favor of something else.  My thinking is that changing the comment is a good idea so that a conversation can happen if someone thinks to start a deprecation process (as the comment currently indicates).

title: BUG: avoid deadlocks using NpyString API
body:
I'm working on a design for a new ByteStringDType and have come across some design issues with StringDType. In particular, it turns out that there are a number of places we're susceptible to possible deadlocks with CPython or between StringDType instances.

For `NpyString_acquire_allocators` and `NpyString_release_allocators`, the fix is to sort the mutexes by address before locking. I added tests for ufuncs that need 2, 3, and 4 allocators as well as one that uses a duplicate allocator that all deadlock on `main` and don't with the fixes here.

There are also a few more fixes:

* StringDType setitem was holding an allocator lock while allowing arbitrary Python code to execute. I added a reentrant example in a test that deadlocks right now.
* There are also issues in several casts with lock discipline and not reliably separating sections of code that hole the allocator lock or use the CPython C API.
* Python 3.12 using `PyThread_type_lock` can deadlock with the GIL, so I added a code that checks if the GIL is held before trying to acquire the lock. This is the same deadlock-avoiding behavior as PyMutex.

There are still places that use the C API with the allocator lock held but I'm pretty sure there are no reentrancy issues in those places.

This was all done heavily with AI assistance. Please let me know if you spot anything you think is fishy because of that.

body: Backport of #31625. DOC: Prevent arrow ligatures in generalized ufunc signatures Bug: #31625 Disable font ligatures for inline code literals so signatures such as ()->() render literally instead of displaying a Unicode arrow glyph in browsers using ligature-enabled fonts. title: BUG: typecode reference leak in array_setstate on 4 error paths (methods.c)
BUG: Reference leak in PyUFunc_GenericReduction on CheckOverride error

labels.name: Priority: low
labels.description: Valid, but not for immediate attention

body:
## Bug Description

In `numpy/_core/src/umath/ufunc_object.c`, when `PyUFunc_CheckOverride` fails in `PyUFunc_GenericReduction`, the code returns NULL directly instead of jumping to the cleanup label, leaking `full_args.in` and `full_args.out`.

## Location

`numpy/_core/src/umath/ufunc_object.c:3777-3780`

## Code

```c
int errval = PyUFunc_CheckOverride(ufunc, _reduce_type[operation],
        full_args.in, full_args.out, wheremask_obj, args, len_args, kwnames, &override);
if (errval) {
    return NULL;    // BUG: should be `goto fail` — leaks full_args.in/out
}
```

## Impact

When `reduce`/`accumulate`/`reduceat` encounters a `__array_ufunc__` override error, the `full_args.in` and `full_args.out` tuple references are leaked. This happens every time an override is attempted on an object that raises an exception in its `__array_ufunc__` implementation.

## Suggested Fix

```c
if (errval) {
    goto fail;  // cleanup path that DECREFs full_args
}
```

## Environment

- NumPy version: current main
- Affected: `np.add.reduce()`, `np.accumulate()` etc. with `__array_ufunc__` overrides that raise

title: BUG: linspace raises ValueError for non-finite values with integer dtype
body:
## Summary

Closes #31651.

`np.linspace` with infinite (or NaN) endpoints and an integer `dtype` silently returns `INT_MIN` for every element instead of raising an error:

```python
np.linspace(np.inf, np.inf, 5, dtype=int)
# array([-9223372036854775808, ...])  ← silent data corruption
```

## Root cause

After the float64 intermediate array is built, `floor()` is called and then `astype(dtype)` converts to the requested integer type. Casting a non-finite float to integer is undefined behaviour in C; on x86-64 it consistently yields `INT_MIN`. NumPy emits a `RuntimeWarning` but does not raise, so callers using `np.errstate(invalid='ignore')` or suppressed warnings receive corrupt data silently.

## Fix

Add a finiteness check immediately after `floor()` (inside the `if integer_dtype:` branch) that raises `ValueError` with a descriptive message before the `astype()` call. Float-dtype paths are completely unaffected.

```python
if integer_dtype:
    if not _nx.isfinite(y).all():
        raise ValueError(
            "Cannot convert non-finite values (inf, -inf, or NaN) to "
            "integer dtype. Use a floating-point dtype or ensure that "
            "start and stop are finite."
        )
    _nx.floor(y, out=y)
```

## Tests

Added `TestLinspace.test_integer_dtype_non_finite_raises` covering:
- `+inf` to `+inf`
- `+inf` to `-inf`
- `-inf` to finite
- `NaN` start
- Regression: normal integer-dtype `linspace(0, 10, 5, dtype=int)` still works

title: BUG: linspace with infinite start/stop and integer dtype silently returns INT_MIN
body:
### Describe the issue:

calling `np.linspace` with `np.inf` (or `-np.inf`) endpoints and an integer `dtype` silently returns `INT_MIN` (`-9223372036854775808`) for every element instead of raising an error. Only a `RuntimeWarning` is emitted an d no exception is raised so the wrong result propagates silently.

I believe the root cause is that the float64 intermediate array ends up containing non-finite values (`inf` or `NaN`, depending on the input combination) before the final cast. Casting a non-finite float to `int64` is undefined behavior in C; on x86-64 this consistently yields `INT_MIN`. NumPy does not validate that `start`/`stop` are finite when `integer_dtype=True` before performing this cast.

Related: #26699 and #17155 .

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import numpy as np

np.linspace(np.inf, np.inf, 5, dtype=int)
# array([-9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808,
#        -9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808])

np.linspace(np.inf, -np.inf, 5, dtype=int)
# array([-9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808,
#        -9223372036854775808, -9223372036854775808])

```
Expected: `ValueError` (infinite values cannot be represented as integers).

### Error message:

```shell
RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in cast
  y = conv.wrap(y.astype(dtype, copy=False))


No exception is raised.
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

2.3.3
3.13.0 (tags/v3.13.0:60403a5, Oct  7 2024, 09:38:07) [MSC v.1941 64 bit (AMD64)]

### Runtime Environment:

_No response_

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

found while auditing edge cases in linspace with integer dtypes. Silent data corruption with no exception, only a RuntimeWarning which means callers using np.errstate(invalid='ignore') or suppressed warnings would receive INT_MIN values with no indication anything went wrong

title: DOC: fix return dtypes in percentile/quantile docstrings
body:
Updated docs to reflect that small floats (like float16) preserve their dtype instead of upcasting to float64. Relates to #31486.

### PR summary
The previous docstrings for `percentile`, `quantile`, `nanpercentile`, and `nanquantile` incorrectly claimed that floating-point inputs smaller than `float64` (such as `float16` and `float32`) are promoted to `float64` in the output. 

Runtime verification confirms that NumPy actually preserves the exact dtype for these floating-point inputs; only integers are upcast. This PR updates the `Returns` block across these four functions to accurately reflect this true runtime behavior while maintaining the original sentence structure.

* Relates to issue #31486 (which highlighted this stale claim for `ma.median`).

**Quick Reproducer:**
```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> arr = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float16)

# OLD DOC CLAIM: The output data-type is `float64`
# ACTUAL RUNTIME BEHAVIOR:
>>> np.percentile(arr, 50).dtype
dtype('float16')
```

### First time committer introduction
Hi everyone! I am an engineering undergrad based in Pune, currently diving deep into machine learning, statistics, and data structures. I use NumPy constantly for my coursework and personal data projects. I was reading through the discussion on #31486, ran some local runtime tests to verify the other functions mentioned there, and wanted to help clean up the rest of this stale documentation family for my first contribution! 

#### AI Disclosure
*I used an AI assistant to locate the stale phrasing across the codebase, but I manually wrote the runtime verifications and formatted the text to comply with NumPy's guidelines.*

title: MAINT: Clean up use for PyObject_* APIs when PyMem_* would do
body:
We were historically a bit sloppy using PyObject_* allocation API for many non-object cases.
This cleans up the rest of those completely, I did change one RawMalloc to not be raw, because the GIL is held and we shouldn't use `RawMalloc` either for this type of allocation.

So this is just a small general improvement (I dunno how bad it is to use the other for non-objects, but I think the Python docs could be clearer about it if it is now on free-threaded).

The original motivation is weird and maybe doesn't matter: The 3.15b2 free-threaded Ubuntu 22.04 builds of the setup-python action fail with segfault for ``PyObject_Realloc(0, ...)``. On the build `PyMem_Realloc()` works fine, so it "solves" the issue although it may be a real issue with the build.

(Of course I am not sure that this is a build issue or a Python issue, I had opened a setup-python issue though.)

(No AI use, just double checked with it I didn't miss anything)

---

I am tempted to backport, just in case the setup-python issue isn't a one-off and because it is trivial.

CC @ngoldbaum in case you are interested about the crash issue.  I suppose @kumaraditya303 could have a brief look to review.

title: DOC: clarify ufunc.at behavior with tuple vs list indices
body:
### PR Summary
Adds an example to the `ufunc.at` documentation showing how
multidimensional indexing works differently.

When using `ufunc.at` on a 2D array, I noticed that passing indices
as a tuple treats them as (row, column) pairs, but passing the same
indices as a list treats them as indices along the first dimension.
The results look very different, and no warning is thrown.

I found this confusing because the difference is not mentioned anywhere
in the docs. This PR adds an example showing both behaviors clearly.

Closes gh-31579

Hi! I am second-year Data Science student and this is my first 
contribution to NumPy.

title: TST: Use pytest.warns as ignore filters+suppress_warnings interfere (#31623)
body:
Backport of #31623.

I am not sure why, it it seems that maybe when used multiple times (and actually capturing?) `suppress_warnings` somehow disrupts the pytest "ignore" filter *only* on free-threaded builds.
(That part is maybe not so weird, since free-threaded builds do more things to make warning filters thread-safe I think.)

I would think it has something to do with messing with `__warning_registery__`, i.e. after the first captured warning we clear it or so and then the second one pytest is in a bad state.

(I feel it's a waste of time to truly understand, as this should be fine)

Either way, it seems just asserting the warning is enough to fix it. One of the tests didn't need it but I added it for symmetry. I omitted `TestWarns`, for some reason it seems unaffected (it only uses `assert_warns()` once per test with actual capture.

**Large diff, but just whitespace, because `pytest.warns` isn't a decorator.**

CC @charris and @ngoldbaum alternative to Chuck's PR that doesn't quite skip them fully but seems to work fine to hide these warnings on free-threaded.

(No AI)

title: BUG: fix incorrect alignment handling and error handling in several code paths (#31615)
body:
Backport of #31615.

Fixes two error paths that are trivially incorrect for OOM scenarios:

* `arr_place` uses `PyArray_ResolveWritebackIfCopy` in an error path, but it probably makes more sense to use `PyArray_DiscardWritebackIfCopy`, as suggested in the docstring for that function: https://numpy.org/doc/2.4/reference/c-api/array.html#c.PyArray_DiscardWritebackIfCopy
* `PyArray_PutTo` and `PyArray_PutMask` fail to check if `PyArray_FromArray` fails.

Fixes an incorrect assumption in the flatiter assignment code - the result array might be a user-supplied unaligned array.

Fixes a logic error in boolean indexing, where if an error is raised during an iteration, the iteration is not halted and it's possible the error could be silently discarded.

Adds tests for the latter two cases.

I used Claude Fable to help out with this. This was spotted during work on #31609 and touches the same functions but the issues are unrelated to StringDType, so I'm issuing this PR separately.

title: DOC: Prevent arrow ligatures in generalized ufunc signatures fix #31625

title: BUG: Fix thread safety issue in f2py allocatable arrays
body:
### PR summary

There were two separate issues:
1. The target data was being passed as a global variable. This means that even assigning individual attributes from different threads is unsafe. Fixed this by passing it through the generated Fortran function call instead.
2. Second (less important), use critical sections to guard the parts where PyFortranObject internals are modified, so that assigning the same attribute from different threads won't corrupt the structure.

I haven't tried to guard anything except the internals of f2py for thread-safety. There's no real point trying to lock the contents of these variables since Fortran itself can access them without the lock.

Also add some tests for allocatable arrays (although not specifically a thread safety test).

This will generate some small merge conflicts with https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/31598 but nothing difficult to fix.

#### AI Disclosure

No AI tools used.

title: TST: Use pytest.warns as ignore filters+suppress_warnings interfere
body:
I am not sure why, it it seems that maybe when used multiple times (and actually capturing?) `suppress_warnings` somehow disrupts the pytest "ignore" filter *only* on free-threaded builds.
(That part is maybe not so weird, since free-threaded builds do more things to make warning filters thread-safe I think.)

I would think it has something to do with messing with `__warning_registery__`, i.e. after the first captured warning we clear it or so and then the second one pytest is in a bad state.

(I feel it's a waste of time to truly understand, as this should be fine)

Either way, it seems just asserting the warning is enough to fix it. One of the tests didn't need it but I added it for symmetry. I omitted `TestWarns`, for some reason it seems unaffected (it only uses `assert_warns()` once per test with actual capture.

**Large diff, but just whitespace, because `pytest.warns` isn't a decorator.**

CC @charris and @ngoldbaum alternative to Chuck's PR that doesn't quite skip them fully but seems to work fine to hide these warnings on free-threaded.

labels.description: PRs and issues related to support for free-threading CPython (a.k.a. no-GIL, PEP 703)

body:
Over in https://github.com/scikit-image/scikit-image/issues/8212, the scikit-image developers are seeing random failures in a test that does some NumPy operations involving OpenBLAS.

Consider the following script:

```python
import threading
import numpy as np

THREADS, ITERS = 12, 50

N = 512 * 512
coords = np.indices((512, 512), dtype=float).reshape(2, -1).T  # non-contiguous
radial = np.random.rand(N, 4)
A = np.random.rand(2, 2)
W = np.random.rand(4, 2)

compute = lambda: coords @ A + radial @ W
expected = compute()

mismatches = 0
lock = threading.Lock()
barrier = threading.Barrier(THREADS)


def worker():
    global mismatches
    count = 0
    for _ in range(ITERS):
        barrier.wait()  # line up all threads on the BLAS call
        if not np.array_equal(compute(), expected):
            count += 1
    with lock:
        mismatches += count


threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(THREADS)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

total = THREADS * ITERS
print(f"{mismatches} mismatches / {total} calls "
      f"({'RACE DETECTED' if mismatches else 'clean'})")

```

title: BUG: Fix interaction between warnings and the promotion cache
body:
Fixes #31758

This fixes an issue that was introduced recently that causes duplicate warnings to be emitted for the integer/timedelta deprecation.

If accessing the promotion cache leads to a miss, the deprecation is emitted to fill the cache and then emitted *again* during type resolution.

This means warnings would sometimes be emitted twice.

The fix is to disable warnings when the promotion cache is filled. This happens using a new context variable. This is all happening outside the hot path for these operations so I'm not worried about performance.

I used Claude Fable to help investigate and fix this issue.

Ping @riku-sakamoto and @may12day since you were both involved in the PR that added these warnings.

title: BUG: fix incorrect alignment handling and error handling in several code paths
body:
Fixes two error paths that are trivially incorrect for OOM scenarios:

* `arr_place` uses `PyArray_ResolveWritebackIfCopy` in an error path, but it probably makes more sense to use `PyArray_DiscardWritebackIfCopy`, as suggested in the docstring for that function: https://numpy.org/doc/2.4/reference/c-api/array.html#c.PyArray_DiscardWritebackIfCopy
* `PyArray_PutTo` and `PyArray_PutMask` fail to check if `PyArray_FromArray` fails.

Fixes an incorrect assumption in the flatiter assignment code - the result array might be a user-supplied unaligned array.

Fixes a logic error in boolean indexing, where if an error is raised during an iteration, the iteration is not halted and it's possible the error could be silently discarded.

Adds tests for the latter two cases.

I used Claude Fable to help out with this. This was spotted during work on #31609 and touches the same functions but the issues are unrelated to StringDType, so I'm issuing this PR separately.

title: BUG: Fix pandas NaT conversion to datetime64 (gh-31608)
body:
### PR summary `np.asarray(pd.NaT).astype('datetime64')` raised `TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer` instead of producing `NaT` (gh-31608). The same failure broke downstream use such as `matplotlib.pyplot.plot(pd.NaT, pd.NaT)`, which otherwise masks missing values like it does for `np.nan`. NumPy converts datetime-like objects by duck typing on their `year`, `month`, and `day` attributes. `pd.NaT` exposes these too, but they return `float('nan')`, so the `PyLong_AsLong` call on the year raised the `TypeError`. This PR detects a NaN `year` in `NpyDatetime_ConvertPyDateTimeToDatetimeStruct` and represents it as NaT using the existing `npy_datetimestruct` convention (`year == NPY_DATETIME_NAT`); `convert_pyobject_to_datetime` then emits the `NPY_DATETIME_NAT` sentinel directly, bypassing unit cast-safety checks just as genuine `datetime64('NaT')` scalars do. --- > ### After the fix > > ```python > >>> np.asarray(pd.NaT).astype('datetime64') > array('NaT', dtype='datetime64[us]') > ``` > > - A `Series` mixing timestamps and `pd.NaT` now converts to a clean `datetime64[ns]` array instead of falling back to `object` dtype. > - Added `TestDateTime::test_datetime_nat_like_object_conversion`, which uses a self-contained duck-typed object with NaN attributes
Test case passes

title: BUG: fix StringDType distinct-allocator bugs and add tests
body:
Fixes bugs when multiple distinct stringdtype arrays are passed to `np.choose`, `np.put`, `np.putmask`, `np.place`, flatiter reads, and a bug that could lead to unsafe views being created for StringDType and object arrays.

Also exposes a new C helper function `_is_safe_view_cast` which takes `view_offset` into account and uses it in the Python helper functions for view safety. It only uses this function for StringDType. We could use it more generally but that might lead to breakage, so just fixing StringDType seemed like a practical first pass.

The C changes all work out to fixing the same couple patterns: legacy paths that used copyswap (e.g. #24859, which this might obviate the need for?) or code paths that assumed all input arrays have the same descriptor instance.

Also adds tests for functionality that is fixed here or is poorly tested currently. It makes use of a new helper function that allocates two distinct arrays of strings with allocations that live in the arena buffer to trigger these bugs.

I milestoned this for 2.5.0 and marked it for backport because these are all bugs that can cause segfaults.

I used Claude Fable 5 to work on this, including for the implementation and new tests.

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

I have a pandas DataFrame that defines the start and end of different definitions of seasons, as indicated by timestamps. Some definitions are not always applicable and are marked with pd.NaT. When I go to plot these indicators as vertical lines against the data, matplotlib should by default masks these missing indicators as it does with nan numeric data but as-is, it just errors. title: BUG: ppc64le: define NPY_HAVE_VSX when only higher VSX levels are enabled
body:
Fixes #31593.

## Problem

On ppc64le, building with `-Dcpu-baseline=none` fails: the VSX dispatch-target
sources hit `implicit declaration of function 'vec_load_len'` (an s390x/VX
intrinsic) and a cascade of undeclared `vec_*` errors, because `<altivec.h>`
is never included.

`NPY_HAVE_VSX` is used throughout the Power SIMD headers as the generic
"any VSX" flag — both to gate the `<altivec.h>` include in
`meson_cpu/main_config.h.in` and to select the Power (vs. s390x/VX) code path
in `simd/vec/*.h`. VSX2/VSX3/VSX4 all imply VSX.

But with an empty baseline, VSX2/3/4 are enabled only as **dispatch targets**,
each compiled in isolation with just its own `NPY_HAVE_VSX{2,3,4}` macro — not
the implied `NPY_HAVE_VSX`. The failing compile line shows `-DNPY_HAVE_VSX2`
with no `-DNPY_HAVE_VSX`. The Power code then falls into the `#else // VX`
branch and `<altivec.h>` is skipped.

Default CI builds don't catch this because the standard ppc64le baseline is
VSX2, which defines `NPY_HAVE_VSX` project-wide; dispatch targets inherit it.

## Fix

Normalize the flag in `meson_cpu/main_config.h.in`: define `NPY_HAVE_VSX`
whenever any of `NPY_HAVE_VSX2/VSX3/VSX4` is defined, before the `<altivec.h>`
include and the SIMD headers consume it.

```c
#if !defined(@P@HAVE_VSX) && (defined(@P@HAVE_VSX2) || defined(@P@HAVE_VSX3) || defined(@P@HAVE_VSX4))
    #define @P@HAVE_VSX 1
#endif
```

The guard is self-gating: it's a no-op on non-Power targets and on any build
that already defines `NPY_HAVE_VSX` (e.g. the default VSX2 baseline). It encodes
the existing implication (VSX2 contains VSX) that the headers already assume.

## Testing

- Minimal reproducer compiles cleanly with the fix; errors without it.
- Full build with `-Dcpu-baseline=none -Dcpu-dispatch=max` on ppc64le (POWER9,
  GCC 15.2) now succeeds; test suite passes (47899 passed, the only failure being
  an unrelated ppc64 long-double string-formatting test,
  `test_ppc64_ibm_double_double128`).

## Alternative considered

Making the meson `features` module propagate implied-feature macros to every
dispatch target generically (which would also help x86 SSE/AVX chains). That's a
larger, riskier change touching the build module; this header-level normalization
is minimal and targeted. Happy to pursue the broader fix if maintainers prefer.

title: BUG: ppc64le build fails with cpu-baseline=none - VSX dispatch targets miss NPY_HAVE_VSX (vec_load_len implicit declaration)
body:
### Describe the issue:

On ppc64le (little-endian POWER), building NumPy with `-Dcpu-baseline=none`
  fails to compile. The VSX dispatch-target sources error out with a cascade of:

  ../numpy/_core/src/common/simd/vec/memory.h:63:12: error: implicit declaration
    of function 'vec_load_len' [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]

  plus `vec_vsx_ld`, `vec_xl`, `vec_vsx_st`, `vec_xst`, `vec_extract`, and many
  `cannot convert a value of type 'int' to vector type ... which has different
  size` follow-ons.

  ### Root cause:

  `vec_load_len` is an **s390x/VX (zarch)** intrinsic, not a Power one. The SIMD
  code in `numpy/_core/src/common/simd/vec/memory.h` selects the right branch via
  `NPY_HAVE_VSX`:

  ```c
  #ifdef NPY_HAVE_VSX
      return vec_promote(*npyv__ptr2u64(ptr), 0);   // Power
  #else // VX
      return vec_load_len((const unsigned long long*)ptr, 7);  // s390x
  #endif

  NPY_HAVE_VSX is the generic "any VSX level" flag, and meson_cpu/main_config.h.in
  only includes <altivec.h> under #ifdef NPY_HAVE_VSX.

  With cpu-baseline=none, VSX2/VSX3/VSX4 are enabled only as dispatch targets.
  Each dispatch target is compiled in isolation with just its own
  -DNPY_HAVE_VSX2 (etc.) and not the implied -DNPY_HAVE_VSX. So on a Power
  build the #else // VX branch is wrongly taken and <altivec.h> is never
  included.

  The actual failing compile command (note -DNPY_HAVE_VSX2 but no
  -DNPY_HAVE_VSX):

  gcc ... -O3 -DNPY_HAVE_VSX2 ... -mcpu=power8 -DNPY_MTARGETS_CURRENT=VSX2 ...
      -c numpy/_core/.../loops_arithmetic.dispatch.c

  This is why default CI builds don't hit it: the default ppc64le baseline is VSX2,
  which defines NPY_HAVE_VSX project-wide via add_project_arguments, so dispatch
  targets inherit it. It only surfaces when the baseline doesn't already include VSX
  (e.g. distributors that set cpu-baseline=none for portable binaries — NixOS does
  this)

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
Minimal standalone reproducer (no NumPy build needed), mirroring npyv__loadl:

  #ifdef NPY_HAVE_VSX
  #  include <altivec.h>
  #endif
  typedef __vector unsigned long long npyv_u64;
  static npyv_u64 npyv__loadl(const void *ptr) {
  #ifdef NPY_HAVE_VSX
      return vec_promote(*(const unsigned long long*)ptr, 0);
  #else /* VX */
      return vec_load_len((const unsigned long long*)ptr, 7);
  #endif
  }
  int main(void){ unsigned long long x[2]={1,2}; npyv__loadl(x); return 0; }

  # fails — simulates a VSX2 dispatch target:
  $ gcc -O3 -mcpu=power8 -DNPY_HAVE_VSX2 -c repro.c
  repro.c: error: implicit declaration of function 'vec_load_len' ...

  # passes — with the implied base flag also defined:
  $ gcc -O3 -mcpu=power8 -DNPY_HAVE_VSX2 -DNPY_HAVE_VSX -c repro.c

  Or, full build: pip install . -Csetup-args=-Dcpu-baseline=none on ppc64le.
```

### Error message:

```shell
../numpy/_core/src/common/simd/vec/memory.h: In function 'npyv__loadl':
  ../numpy/_core/src/common/simd/vec/memory.h:63:12: error: implicit declaration
    of function 'vec_load_len' [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
     63 |     return vec_load_len((const unsigned long long*)ptr, 7);
        |            ^~~~~~~~~~~~
  ... (vec_vsx_ld, vec_xl, vec_vsx_st, vec_xst, vec_extract, and
  "cannot convert a value of type 'int' to vector type" cascades)
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

NumPy v2.4.4 (also present on main). Python 3.13.

### Runtime Environment:

ppc64le (little-endian, POWER9), Linux. GCC 15.2 and GCC 16.1 both reproduce.
  Build configured with -Dcpu-baseline=none -Dcpu-dispatch=max.

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

_No response_

title: BUG: raise a clear error in common_type for non-array input
body:
Fixes #30890

## Summary

`numpy.common_type` does `a.dtype.type` on each input so passing a dtype or a scalar type, for example `np.common_type(np.dtype("f4"))`, raised a confusing `AttributeError` (`'numpy.dtypes.Float32DType' object has no attribute 'dtype'`).

This catches that case and raises a `TypeError` that points to `np.result_type` and `np.promote_types` which are the tools meant for combining dtypes and scalar types. A dtype instance is shown as `dtype('float32')` and a scalar type as `'float32'`. Valid array inputs are unchanged. This follows the direction @ngoldbaum and @seberg suggested on the issue.

Before:
```
>>> np.common_type(np.dtype("f4"))
AttributeError: 'numpy.dtypes.Float32DType' object has no attribute 'dtype'
```
After:
```
>>> np.common_type(np.dtype("f4"))
TypeError: common_type takes array inputs, not dtype('float32'). To find a common type for dtypes or scalar types use np.result_type or np.promote_types instead.
```

## Test plan

Added tests in `numpy/lib/tests/test_type_check.py` for dtype and scalar-type inputs: a clear `TypeError` with the `np.result_type` / `np.promote_types` guidance, the dtype instance shown as `dtype('float32')`, and the scalar type as `'float32'`. Existing `TestCommonType.test_basic` still covers real arrays. Release note added in `doc/release/upcoming_changes/30890.improvement.rst`.

This change was prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex). I reviewed and verified the change and the tests locally and take responsibility for it.

title: BUG: (Linux) Setting MADV_HUGEPAGE on heap allocations can adversely affect the behavior of later allocations
body:
### Describe the issue:

On Linux, Numpy calls madvise with MADV_HUGEPAGE on memory returned by the heap allocator:
https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/6e0d988e591b697abb1dcfbe37043e2853d63acd/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/alloc.c#L116

That memory is later returned to the allocator without unsetting that bit (which AFAICT, Linux does not provides a way to do - MADV_NOHUGEPAGE is not the opposite of MADV_HUGEPAGE). This alters the behavior of that memory region beyond the lifetime of numpy's allocation. Setting MADV_HUGEPAGE can sometimes result in pretty disastrous performance degradations when the allocator later hands out that memory to somebody else. In particular, if /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag  is `defer+madvise` or `madvise` and a memory region tagged with MADV_HUGEPAGE is faulted in while the system has no hugepages available, Linux can stall on running a synchronous reclaim/compaction process instead of falling back to non-hugepages. https://github.com/golang/go/issues/61718 discusses a similar perf regression in Go.

Unfortunately, I don't have any great ideas for a fix that would make everybody happy. Linux doesn't seem to expose an API that lets you undo the effect of madvise with MADV_HUGEPAGE on a mapping (or a better API than /proc/pid/smaps for querying the disposition of a memory region).

There's an argument for disabling this codepath when /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled is "always" since in that config, Linux will already make a best effort to use hugepages by default. That is only a partial improvement though - it wouldn't do much for folks running under different configs.

One might consider allocating large arrays with mmap so that calling madvise does not pollute the state of memory owned by the heap allocator, but that can be much slower than using the heap allocator, which doesn't seem ideal.

There is an MADV_COLLAPSE madvise option that doesn't permanently change the state of a memory region, but that also looks fairly heavyweight (it seems like Go folks tried using it and ended up reverting it due to perf regressions).

Just wanted to raise this issue so in case anybody else runs into it - it was surprising to find out that a library was changing settings on memory regions in a way that would affect later unrelated heap allocations!

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
Happens on Linux by default when allocating an array with size >= 2MB
```

### Error message:

```shell

```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

The behavior was introduced in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/11919.

### Runtime Environment:

_No response_

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

This was found when debugging process stalls due to Linux's synchronous reclaim/compaction on a system with /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag  set to `defer+madvise`. The system was low on hugepages due to memory fragmentation, but had regular pages available. Were it not for this issue, Linux should have fallen back to regular pages instead of stalling.

title: guard isdigit calls against non-ascii in str_to_int parsers
body:
loadtxt parses integer fields from a Py_UCS4 buffer, but the digit checks hand raw code points to ctype isdigit():
- str_to_int64 calls isdigit(*p) and isdigit(d) on Py_UCS4 values
- str_to_uint64 does the same in its digit loop
- isdigit is only defined for unsigned char or EOF, so a code point above 255 (e.g. U+0100 in an int column) indexes the ctype table out of bounds on glibc
gated all five checks behind an ascii-range helper.

title: NumPy 1.16.6+security.2: backport CVE-2021-41496 (f2py array_from_pyobj)
body:
ActiveState security release on the 1.16.6 line (DE-8118).

## Fixed
- **CVE-2021-41496** (GHSA-f7c7-j99h-c22f) — stack buffer overflow in the f2py `array_from_pyobj` error path: it built a "must have defined dimensions" message into a fixed 200-byte `mess[]` buffer via `strcpy` + a `sprintf` loop over up to `F2PY_MAX_DIMS` (40) dims + `strcat`, which can overflow with enough negative dimensions (local DoS). Backported upstream `271010f1037150e9` (PR numpy/numpy#20630, closes gh-19000): replaces `count_negative_dimensions()` with `find_first_negative_dimension()` and emits a single bounded `PyErr_Format()`. Kept a C89-style loop var for older-MSVC compatibility (cf. the CVE-2021-41495 compiler fixups).

## Assessed — not applicable (table-only)
- **CVE-2021-33430** (GHSA-6p56-wp2h-9hxr) — already mitigated here: the `nd > NPY_MAXDIMS` guard is present at `ctors.c:934`, ahead of the `descr->subarray` `memcpy`.
- **CVE-2021-34141** (GHSA-fpfv-jqm9-f5jm) — disputed; the deprecated Numeric-style typecode `strncmp` only affects a `DeprecationWarning`, not the resolved dtype. No upstream security fix.

## Release
- Version bumped to the PEP 440 local form **`1.16.6+security.2`** in `setup.py` so the installed package self-reports the security level (`1.16.6.1` == security.1).
- Added `doc/release/1.16.6+security.2-notes.rst` + changelog.

## Validation
C89 syntax-checked (incl. `-Wdeclaration-after-statement`); `setup.py` compiles and reports `1.16.6+security.2`; `NumpyVersion()` tolerates the `+local` label. The f2py change is not runnable in this environment (build-generated `_numpyconfig.h`); it relies on the build pipeline (upstream shipped the same change without an added test).

title: MAINT: Use Python C API functions for f2py error formatting
body:
### PR summary

My original interest here was to eliminate the non-limited API access to `->tp_name` (and thus it's kind of part of https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/21300). However, looking at what I was changing, it seemed like a large amount of C string handling could be removed in the process (and because the result inevitably ends up in Python strings, I don't think this is any less efficient).

The main effect is to eliminate a bunch of fixed-size string buffers and the possibility for overflowing those.

Hopefully most of the output should be identical. There's one place where I've updated a test because the output is slightly different and the old version really didn't make sense to me.

All code and text was written by me. I used copilot to find a silly mistake I'd made that was causing it to crash (because I couldn't get `gdb` and `spin` to cooperate here) and to sanity check what I'd done.

title: DOC: ufunc.add behaves differently with indices as tuple and list/array
body:
### Issue with current documentation:

It comes fairly non-intuitive to me that the `ufunc.at` operates very differently when indices are provided either as array or list, or as a tuple. 

In first two cases, apparently they are taken as 1D indices (and applied multiple times to entire rows). Taking transpose of the array has no effect.

In the third case, when a tuple is provided, they are used as expected, i.e., as 2D indices.

```Python
In [1]: ar = np.zeros([3,3]); np.add.at(ar, np.array([[0,1,2],[0,1,2]]), 1); print(ar)
[[2. 2. 2.]
 [2. 2. 2.]
 [2. 2. 2.]]

In [2]: ar = np.zeros([3,3]); np.add.at(ar, [[0,1,2],[0,1,2]], 1); print(ar)
[[2. 2. 2.]
 [2. 2. 2.]
 [2. 2. 2.]]

In [3]: ar = np.zeros([3,3]); np.add.at(ar, ([0,1,2],[0,1,2]), 1); print(ar)
[[1. 0. 0.]
 [0. 1. 0.]
 [0. 0. 1.]]

```

This is quite an insidious difference in behaviour, particularly because:
* The numerically different result has same data type and shape in all cases, and is given without any explicit warning. Thus it might only manifest itself later in other parts of Python code not working properly.
* Many functions in Python ecosystem use duck typing and strive behave consistently for compound data types. Accordingly, many people, including me, seem to think about tuples just as an immutable, more efficient alternative to a list. Replacing one with another may cause errors sometimes, but should not redefine function behaviour.
* Many others may stick to numpy arrays everywhere for the sake of consistency. They may never get the idea that they should convert their np.array indices to a tuple. 


### Idea or request for content:

* I believe this **difference should be described in the docs** https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ufunc.at.html (at least in the Examples section)
* As it is seemingly unlikely that anybody would index 1D arrays by a list-of-lists containing the 1D indices, the **function should throw a warning about potentially undesired result**. Anybody wanting exactly this behaviour can easily suppress this warning by explicitly concatenating the 1D indices, i.e. using `[[0,1,2, 0,1,2]]` or equivalently `np.hstack([[0,1,2], [0,1,2]])` instead of `[[0,1,2],[0,1,2]]` in the above examples.

title: PERF, BUG: speed up conversion of Python datetime/date to datetime64, handle duck-type datetime objects
body:
`NpyDatetime_ConvertPyDateTimeToDatetimeStruct` is the per-element worker behind casting object arrays of Python datetimes to `datetime64`, e.g. `np.asarray(list_of_datetimes).astype("M8[us]")` (the floor of matplotlib's `date2num`, and relevant to pandas/xarray too).

This PR makes two complementary changes:

- **Fast path:** for genuine `datetime.date` / `datetime.datetime` objects
  (including subclasses such as pandas `Timestamp`), read the fields straight from
  the CPython C struct via the datetime C-API macros 
- **Cheaper attribute access** for the remaining cases: the duck-typed fallback and
  the per-element `tzinfo` lookup now use a single `PyObject_GetOptionalAttr` on
  pre-interned attribute names (added to `npy_interned_str`). The `tzinfo`
  lookup runs for every datetime

Benchmark

| cast | before | after | speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `datetime.datetime` → `M8[us]` | ~1130 ns | ~52 ns | ~21x |
| `datetime.date` → `M8[D]` | ~490 ns | ~38 ns | ~13x |

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script and notes</summary>

```python
import time, datetime, numpy as np

def best(fn, R=20000, trials=9):
    fn()
    ts = []
    for _ in range(trials):
        s = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(R):
            fn()
        ts.append(time.perf_counter() - s)
    return min(ts) / R

N = 100
dts = [datetime.datetime(2000, 1, 1) + datetime.timedelta(seconds=i * 1234567)
       for i in range(N)]
a = np.asarray(dts)
dates = [datetime.date(2000, 1, 1) + datetime.timedelta(days=i) for i in range(N)]
ad = np.asarray(dates)
base = np.arange(1000.0)  # unrelated op, sanity-check for binary-layout noise

print("dt   ->M8[us]: %6.1f ns/elem" % (best(lambda: a.astype('M8[us]')) / N * 1e9))
print("date ->M8[D] : %6.1f ns/elem" % (best(lambda: ad.astype('M8[D]')) / N * 1e9))
print("baseline sum : %6.1f ns"      % (best(lambda: base.sum()) * 1e9))
```

</details>

title: BUG: Fix order of real and imaginary NaNs when sorting complex in descending order (#31557)
body:
Backport of #31557.


Fixes a bug from #31345 where complex numbers with only imaginary nans get sorted _before_ those with only real nans in descending sorts, when keeping in with our NaN semantics they should be sorted _after_ (real nans are the primary key). This should probably be backported to 2.5, cc @seberg @charris

The longstanding `less` implementation is a bit confusing, but I didn't refactor/simplify and kept this change minimal. It would be good to confirm this is the correct behavior, though, as the `greater` is a bit hard to read (hopefully less so now):

1. if greater, only push to right if the imaginary part is strictly NaN but the other is not,
2. if less, only push to right if the _other_ imaginary part is strictly NaN but _this_ one is not,
3. If real parts are equal or _both_ are NaN, break the tie by float-like comparison of imaginary,
4. Failing all (i.e., only _one_ of the real parts is NaN), push to the right only if first is NaN.

So for the real part at least:

* If both reals are non-NaN -> branch 1-2
* If exactly one real is NaN -> branch 4
* If both reals are NaN -> branch 3

Sorry, verbose, but hopefully that clears things, thank you for reviewing!

No AI tools used.

title: BUG,TST: Fix condition for whether long double is “IBM double double” (#31375)
body:
Backport of #31375.

Some distributions changed the default for long double on 64-bit PowerPC (at least little-endian) from the “IBM double double” format to the IEEE 754 binary128 format. The implementation already handles that by detecting the format at build time (longdouble_format property). Before this change, the tests checked only the CPU architecture name, possibly falsely assuming that long double has the “IBM double double” format when it actually has the IEEE 754 binary128 format. After this change, the tests assume the “IBM double double” format only if the maximum value, determined by calling numpy.finfo(), is the maximum value characteristic for the “IBM double double” format. On CPU architectures other than PowerPC, the “IBM double double” format is never assumed. I found no evidence that any other CPU architecture ever used that format.

On a system where long double has the “IBM double double” format, the test results don’t change:

47406 passed, 1047 skipped, 2845 deselected, 32 xfailed, 4 xpassed

On a system where long double has the IEEE 754 binary128 format, the test results change from:

1 failed, 47404 passed, 1049 skipped, 2845 deselected, 32 xfailed, 4 xpassed

to:

47408 passed, 1048 skipped, 2845 deselected, 32 xfailed, 2 xpassed

Fixes #21094.

### First time committer introduction

I rarely use NumPy directly. I encountered one of the previous test failures when building the NumPy package in the Nix package collection (which runs the tests).
